title: I Used the Steel-Pan Checkout on the Captain Who Hijacked My Numbered Tenor

parts.text: I stepped into the pan yard at 6:08 p.m. and captain Rhea was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE TENOR. TWO HOURS. PANS STAY WITH THE CHECKOUT. I was twenty-eight, yard secretary, holding a clipboard that listed our numbered tenor. Rhea shrugged. "Captains are the yard." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover sticks on my numbered tenor. Then I asked for the pan log. At 6:16 the shed pinged why Rhea's name was on my skirt. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The shed can see Rhea's leftover sticks on my numbered tenor.

social.video_title: She hijacked my numbered tenor on my checkout — Part 1/2
social.description: Pan yard, leftover sticks, a two-hour clock she posted. I logged the skirt. Would you have asked for the pan log?

parts.text: Rhea called it tune-up until the shed asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the stick still. The tenor went back to my numbered checkout. Rhea ran a slot of her own and told the next captain atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: CAPTAINS ARE NOT THE YARD. I keep my pan on a labeled hook. Rhea brown-bags her tune-ups. The yard finally looks like a checkout, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Captains are not the yard — Part 2/2
social.description: Pan log, numbered tenor, and a second line on the board. Was a tune-up ever my skirt?
